notes: Ellingham's arc shows in whose hand the paper is written in: when the Major holds the room he takes dictation, and when the housekeeper's hours look like evidence he writes them himself and asks you to initial. The topic the story turns on is the will, the old one he means to stand and the new one he drafted and never had signed.

description.text: He has moved his chair so that you stand between him and the Major, and when an hour is given he writes it and turns the sheet toward you, pen out, for an initial. He never asks the Major to initial anything.

He writes with his head down and the Major at his shoulder, and the hours going onto the page are the Major's, read off a watch. When you pass behind him he turns the sheet face down, not quickly, as a man tidies.

Your hours are in his inside pocket now; his hand goes to the lapel when the Major raises his voice, and comes away again. The rest of his papers lie open on the table as if to show there is nothing else to find.

There is one folded sheet he keeps apart from the pile, under the lid of the writing case, and he has stopped writing the doctor's words halfway down it. He looks at the Major a moment longer than a man looks at an old client.

Past sixty, narrow, black coat gone green at the seams, spectacles pushed up when he listens and down when he writes. He addresses you as Mrs and not by your office, and asks what time a thing was before he asks what it was.

here.text: Ellingham keeps his papers squared under one hand and his pen capped, and does not look up when you come in.
Ellingham has his portable writing case open on his knees and a pen already inked, waiting for somebody to give him an hour.

says.text: 'A draft is not an instrument. It expresses what a man was minded to do on a Tuesday, and he was free to be minded otherwise on the Wednesday, and he died on neither.' He does not look at the writing case. 'We had an understanding on the gallery, Mrs. I have kept my half.'

'The will that stands is the one that is signed, witnessed and in my keeping, and that is the will of eighteen-seventy, in Mr Yardley's favour.' He caps the pen. 'Has anyone in this house told you there is another? I ask because I should like to know who is saying so.'

'There is a will, it is executed, and it is lodged with my firm. Beyond that a housekeeper has no need to go, and I say that without discourtesy.' He waits to see whether you will go beyond it anyway.

'He bolts when he is looked at; it is a habit, not a confession, though a magistrate may not distinguish. I should want to know what hour he was in the yard before I say more, and who has said it besides you.'

'The nephew inherits under the will as it stands. That is a fact, not an opinion, and I give it because facts are the only thing I am paid to give.' He lets the pen rest. 'What has the Major said of him to you?'

'Major Carrington is executor in all but name, and he is the master's oldest friend, and he has a watch.' He draws a line under something. 'None of those three things is evidence, and I should be obliged if you did not repeat that I said so.'

'He gives his hours very readily. I have noticed that men who give hours readily have usually fixed them beforehand, which is not the same as having lied.' He looks at the door. 'Where was he at eleven, by your rounds?'

'Your rounds are the only account in this house that was written before anyone knew there was a death to account for. That makes them worth more than the Major's watch, and he knows it, which is why he wants them in his hand and not mine.' He holds out the pen. 'Initial each hour, if you please.'

'A housekeeper's book is kept nightly and in course of duty, and a court will take it over any gentleman's recollection, provided it has not been added to since.' He turns to the murder night and runs his finger down it. 'Has it?'

'Dr Ashcombe says the master knew his time and sent for the Major, and I have written that down because I was asked to, not because I know what it is for.' He folds the sheet once. 'A dying man who sends for a friend generally sends for a solicitor the same week. He did not send for me.'

portrait.composition: Medium bust portrait, three-quarter angle, seated slightly forward over a writing case with pen lifted, head tilted as if listening for an hour
subjects: Thin lined face, pale grey eyes behind small steel spectacles pushed up on the forehead
Ink stain on the right forefinger, dry papery hands
White side-whiskers, hair thin and combed flat
Gaze sidelong and patient, assessing rather than meeting
